CurrentText: This study examines the economic effect of EV-supported export in a residential PV-battery-EV scheduling model using one prepared House1 dataset from 13 June to 2 October 2014. Corrected V2H and export-enabled V2G share cost-minus-revenue accounting; V2G additionally permits EV-supported export. The 24-hour formulation includes day-specific availability, trip withdrawal and a first-trip energy equality, but no terminal EV-SOC restoration. Of 90 attempted days, 74 form common valid corrected-regime pairs. V2G has a lower pre-restoration net operating cost on all 74 valid pairs, with a mean saving of £0.509/day. Negative pre-restoration V2G operating cost occurs in 43 of the 74 valid cases (58.1%), although the mean V2G operating cost remains positive. Additional export revenue, rather than reduced gross import, explains this pre-restoration effect. Symmetric post-optimisation restoration accounting reverses the base comparison: mean adjusted V2G saving is −£0.632/day, with lower adjusted V2G cost on 0/74 pairs. This adjustment is not terminal-constrained re-optimisation or proof of a feasible restoration schedule. Independent tariff and EV-capacity re-optimisations demonstrate scenario dependence, while degradation sensitivity and Monte Carlo results are fixed-dispatch accounting. The findings are conditional on the household profiles, tariffs, mobility and availability inputs, EV-export permission and degradation proxy. They identify a short-horizon export-revenue mechanism, not universal V2G profitability or a repeatable household investment case.

CurrentText: F. Practical and Network Interpretation
RequiredAction: REPLACE affected results/captions with certified R2.2 tables and figures; historical numerical evidence is not current

CurrentText: From a future tariff- and policy-design perspective, the results identify several variables that require joint consideration rather than treating export remuneration in isolation. First, the strong dependence of pre-restoration V2G economics on export revenue indicates that the import/export price relationship can materially alter the optimiser’s use of the EV and the resulting grid exchange. Second, the increase in EV degradation cost shows that export remuneration should be interpreted together with the cost of battery utilisation. Third, the terminal-SOC analysis demonstrates that an apparent short-horizon export benefit can reverse when the energy required to restore the EV is accounted for. Accordingly, evaluations of future V2G tariff structures should distinguish between gross export revenue, battery-wear cost, mobility requirements and the value of end-of-horizon stored energy.
RequiredAction: REPLACE affected results/captions with certified R2.2 tables and figures; historical numerical evidence is not current

CurrentText: The results also indicate that tariff design cannot be considered independently of distribution-network conditions. Export-enabled V2G substantially increases household-boundary export, while the present model does not verify feeder voltage, transformer loading, reverse-power-flow limits or hosting capacity. Future V2G frameworks could therefore evaluate price signals together with explicit network constraints, export limits or other network-aware operating conditions. These findings do not prescribe a particular tariff or regulatory mechanism; rather, they identify the economic and physical factors that should be represented when assessing alternative V2G market and tariff structures.

CurrentText: Export capacity is another potentially important constraint, but a physically valid export-limit sensitivity requires the export-power bound to be imposed at every scheduling interval and the optimisation to be re-solved. The present study does not provide such a re-optimised export-cap experiment and therefore does not claim quantitative performance under specific 6 kW, 3.68 kW, 1.5 kW or zero-export limits. In practical deployment, tighter export limits would restrict one of the principal mechanisms generating the pre-restoration V2G cost difference and could alter both dispatch and revenue; the magnitude of that effect must be determined through explicit constrained re-optimisation.

RequiredAction: REPLACE affected results/captions with certified R2.2 tables and figures; historical numerical evidence is not current

CurrentText: The household-level results demonstrate that export-enabled V2G can substantially increase power exchanged with the grid boundary, but this increase should not be interpreted automatically as a distribution-network benefit. The present optimisation represents the utility grid as an import/export boundary and does not model the upstream low-voltage feeder, distribution transformer, node voltages, phase imbalance, line thermal limits or network power flow. Consequently, the present results establish household-level economic and dispatch behaviour rather than network-level hosting capacity or operational acceptability.

CurrentText: Previous distribution-network studies show why these effects cannot be inferred from a household optimisation alone. Coordinated EV charging has been shown to require explicit consideration of low-voltage network constraints, including voltage and equipment loading, while V2G-based control has also been investigated as a means of supporting distribution-voltage regulation when vehicle operation is coordinated with network conditions [17]. More recent network studies similarly identify transformer capacity, feeder loading, voltage limits and hosting capacity as relevant constraints when EV and V2G penetration increases.

CurrentText: The direction of the network effect is therefore context dependent. Export from V2G can potentially support the network when discharge is coordinated with local demand or voltage-control requirements, but poorly coordinated or highly coincident export can also increase reverse power flow, raise local voltages, or increase utilisation of transformers and feeders. Accordingly, a household schedule that is economically attractive under an unrestricted grid-boundary model may not remain feasible if feeder-specific voltage or thermal constraints are imposed.

Relevant mechanisms include interval-dependent export limits, dynamic operating envelopes, transformer-loading constraints, feeder-voltage constraints and network-aware V2G scheduling. These controls could reduce the quantity or alter the timing of export and would therefore modify both dispatch and household revenue relative to the unconstrained grid-boundary results reported here.
